# Confirming Supersymmetry Through Spin Measurements: The Case of the Sbottom Quark

## The Challenge of Establishing a Supersymmetric Origin

The discovery of new particles beyond the Standard Model at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) would represent a landmark achievement in particle physics, but such a discovery alone would not be sufficient to establish that these particles are genuinely supersymmetric in nature. Supersymmetry (SUSY) makes a very specific prediction: for every Standard Model particle, there exists a superpartner whose spin differs by exactly one-half unit. Verifying this prediction requires more than simply detecting new massive states consistent with the SUSY particle spectrum; it demands a detailed characterization of their quantum numbers—particularly their spins—as well as their couplings to Standard Model particles. This is because several alternative theoretical frameworks, such as models with universal extra dimensions (UED), predict particle spectra that can closely mimic the SUSY mass hierarchy while assigning entirely different spin quantum numbers to the new states. Without a spin measurement, a discovery of new heavy particles could be equally consistent with either scenario, leaving the fundamental question of supersymmetry unresolved.

## Probing the Spin of the Sbottom Quark

One particularly interesting test case is the bottom squark, or sbottom, the supersymmetric partner of the Standard Model bottom quark. In supersymmetric theories, the sbottom is a scalar (spin-0) particle, whereas in UED-type models, the corresponding new state—often referred to as a heavy bottom quark partner—is a fermion (spin-1/2), analogous to a Kaluza-Klein excitation of the bottom quark. Distinguishing between these two possibilities is essential for confirming the supersymmetric nature of any observed signal in the sbottom sector.

At the LHC, this spin determination can be accomplished through the study of sbottom pair production, followed by an analysis of the angular correlations among the visible decay products. The underlying strategy exploits the fact that the spin of the pair-produced particle influences the angular distribution and correlation patterns of its decay products in a way that is sensitive to whether the parent particle is a scalar or a fermion. By carefully reconstructing these angular observables on an event-by-event basis, one can statistically discriminate between the spin hypotheses associated with the supersymmetric and the extra-dimensional interpretations.

## The Decay Channel and Its Angular Signature

The specific channel exploited for this analysis is the decay of each produced sbottom into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino, the latter typically assumed to be the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) and thus stable on collider timescales, escaping detection as missing transverse energy. In pair-production events, both sbottoms decay through this channel, yielding a final state containing two bottom quarks accompanied by missing energy carried away by the neutralinos. The angular correlations between the two bottom-quark jets—arising from the spin-dependent dynamics of the production and decay process—encode information about the spin of the intermediate sbottom state. In the supersymmetric case, the scalar nature of the sbottom implies the absence of any preferred spin-correlation structure inherited from the production mechanism, since a spin-0 particle cannot transmit spin information to its decay products. By contrast, in the UED scenario, the fermionic nature of the heavy bottom quark partner allows spin correlations from the production process to propagate through to the final-state angular distributions, resulting in a measurably different correlation pattern.

## Discriminating Power and Experimental Feasibility

This angular correlation technique therefore provides a powerful and, in principle, clean method for distinguishing between the competing spin hypotheses: it directly probes whether the new particle behaves as a boson, consistent with supersymmetry, or as a fermion, consistent with universal extra dimensions. In practice, however, the successful application of this method depends critically on two experimental factors: the production cross section for sbottom pairs must be sufficiently large to yield an adequate sample of events, and the branching ratio for the sbottom decay into a bottom quark plus neutralino must be sizable enough that the resulting signal can be efficiently extracted from the substantial Standard Model backgrounds—most notably those arising from top-quark pair production and other processes yielding bottom-quark jets alongside missing transverse energy. When these conditions are met, the angular correlation analysis in the sbottom pair production channel offers a robust and largely model-independent handle on the spin of the sbottom, providing crucial confirmatory evidence for the supersymmetric interpretation of any new physics signal observed at the LHC.

# Distinguishing Sbottom Spin at the LHC: A Study of Angular Correlations

## Introduction

The discovery of a new particle beyond the Standard Model would represent only the first step in understanding the underlying physics. Equally important is determining the fundamental properties of any such particle, including its mass, couplings, and—critically—its spin. Spin determination is essential for distinguishing between competing theoretical frameworks that might otherwise produce similar signatures at collider experiments. This paper addresses precisely this challenge: differentiating between two well-motivated scenarios that predict superficially similar collider phenomenology.

## The Physics Challenge

Supersymmetry (SUSY) predicts a bosonic partner for every Standard Model fermion. In particular, the superpartner of the bottom quark—the sbottom (denoted $\tilde{b}$)—is a scalar particle (spin-0). Competing scenarios, most notably models with universal extra dimensions (UED), predict that new colored particles appearing at the same mass scale would instead be fermions, specifically Kaluza-Klein excitations of the bottom quark with the same quantum numbers under the Standard Model gauge group.

If discovered, the sbottom would be expected to decay predominantly into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino, $\tilde{\chi}_1^0$, which serves as a natural dark matter candidate in many SUSY models. This decay chain,

$$\tilde{b} \to b + \tilde{\chi}_1^0,$$

produces final states that are essentially indistinguishable from those expected in the fermionic UED scenario at the level of particle content and basic kinematics. Since many observables—masses, production cross sections, and missing energy signatures—can mimic one another between these two possibilities, a method is needed to unambiguously establish the spin of the produced particle.

## The Method: Angular Correlations in Pair Production

The central proposal of this analysis is to exploit angular correlations in sbottom pair production and decay to probe the underlying spin structure. Since $\tilde{b}\tilde{b}^*$ pairs are produced via quark-quark annihilation or gluon fusion at the LHC, the angular distributions of the outgoing decay products—particularly the bottom quarks and any accompanying invisible neutralinos—carry direct information about the spin of the intermediate state.

For scalar sbottoms, the underlying production process proceeds without preferred spin correlations between the two produced particles, and the subsequent two-body decay $\tilde{b} \to b\,\tilde{\chi}_1^0$ yields angular distributions of the visible bottom quark that reflect this scalar nature. In contrast, in the UED scenario, the fermionic nature of the KK-quark partner induces a distinct pattern of angular correlations, tied to the spin-1/2 nature of the particle and its coupling structure to the KK photon (the UED analog of the neutralino).

By carefully constructing kinematic variables—such as angular distributions of the bottom quarks relative to the production axis, or correlations between the two decay chains in the pair-produced system—one can build discriminating observables sensitive to the spin of the intermediate particle. These observables are largely independent of the detailed mass spectrum, making them robust probes of spin even when only the overall mass scale is known from initial measurements of missing transverse energy or invariant mass edges.

## Analysis and Results

The study performs a detailed Monte Carlo analysis of the process:

$$pp \to \tilde{b}\tilde{b}^* \to b\bar{b} + \tilde{\chi}_1^0\tilde{\chi}_1^0$$

at LHC energies, comparing the resulting angular distributions to those predicted in the corresponding fermionic UED scenario with matched mass parameters. The analysis includes realistic treatment of detector effects, combinatorial backgrounds from jet assignment, and the dominant Standard Model backgrounds, including top quark pair production and $Z$+jets processes, which can mimic the $b\bar{b}$ plus missing energy signature.

The results demonstrate that the proposed angular correlation technique can successfully distinguish the scalar (SUSY) hypothesis from the fermionic (UED) hypothesis, provided sufficient statistics are available. Specifically, the analysis finds that:

- The discriminating power of the angular observables is robust across a range of sbottom and neutralino mass combinations relevant to natural SUSY scenarios.
- Standard Model backgrounds, while significant, can be sufficiently suppressed through appropriate kinematic cuts without eliminating the spin-sensitive signal.
- The method's sensitivity depends critically on the sbottom pair production cross section and the branching ratio to the $b + \tilde{\chi}_1^0$ final state. When these are sufficiently large, a statistically significant signal emerges above background within achievable LHC luminosities.

## Conclusion

This work establishes that measuring angular correlations in sbottom pair production offers a viable strategy for confirming the bosonic nature of the sbottom, thereby providing genuine evidence for supersymmetry rather than merely detecting a new particle with SUSY-like quantum numbers. This capability is particularly valuable for resolving the potential confusion between SUSY and UED scenarios, which can otherwise produce very similar missing energy signatures and mass spectra. The key limiting factor for applying this method at the LHC is not the intrinsic discriminating power of the angular variables themselves, but rather ensuring sufficient signal statistics through adequate production rates and decay branching fractions. When these conditions are met, this channel provides a clear, robust experimental handle on the spin of the sbottom, contributing to the broader program of confirming supersymmetry through detailed characterization of new physics states beyond simple discovery.

# Establishing CERN's Large-Scale Scientific Infrastructure

The European Organization for Nuclear Research, known as CERN, stands as one of the most remarkable achievements in the history of international scientific collaboration. Established in 1954 in the aftermath of World War II, CERN was founded on a bold vision: that scientific advancement, particularly in the realm of fundamental physics, could serve as a unifying force for European nations recovering from conflict and division.

The process of establishing CERN required unprecedented cooperation among twelve founding member states, who recognized that no single nation could independently support the enormous costs and infrastructure needed for large-scale particle physics research. This collaborative model became a template for international scientific ventures that followed.

What makes CERN truly exceptional is the scale of its infrastructure. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC), completed in 2008, represents the crowning achievement of this ambitious enterprise. Spanning a 27-kilometer circumference tunnel beneath the Franco-Swiss border, the LHC stands as the largest and most powerful particle accelerator ever constructed. This massive machine allows scientists to recreate conditions similar to those that existed fractions of a second after the Big Bang, accelerating particles to nearly the speed of light before colliding them together.

The establishment of such large-scale infrastructure has yielded extraordinary scientific returns. Most notably, the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed a fundamental particle that had been theoretically predicted decades earlier, completing the Standard Model of particle physics and earning the Nobel Prize in Physics for the theorists who had predicted its existence.

Beyond its scientific contributions, CERN's establishment demonstrated how large-scale international cooperation could produce infrastructure and knowledge beyond the reach of any single nation. The organization also gave birth to another world-changing innovation: the World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 while working at CERN to help scientists share information more effectively.

Today, CERN continues to exemplify how establishing large, complex scientific infrastructure through international cooperation can push the boundaries of human knowledge, inspiring similar collaborative megaprojects across various scientific disciplines worldwide.

# Abstract

We investigate strategies for determining the spin of the scalar bottom quark (sbottom) at the Large Hadron Collider, providing a means to distinguish supersymmetric models from scenarios with universal extra dimensions (UED), where the sbottom's Kaluza-Klein analog carries different spin quantum numbers. Both theoretical frameworks predict similar particle spectra and comparable production cross sections at the LHC, making spin determination a crucial handle for discriminating between these competing new physics scenarios rather than relying solely on mass measurements.

We focus on the decay chain in which sbottom pair production is followed by decays through a chargino to a top quark and neutralino-like state, i.e., $\tilde{b} \to t + \chi^-_1 \to t + (W^- + \chi^0_1)$, or its charge-conjugate, yielding final states with top quarks, W bosons, and missing transverse energy from the stable neutral particle. We construct invariant mass distributions and angular correlations among the visible decay products—particularly the charge asymmetry in invariant mass distributions involving the top quark and the intermediate chargino-like state—that are sensitive to the spin of the sbottom and its superpartners in the decay chain.

Using Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate realistic detector effects, parton distribution functions, and relevant Standard Model backgrounds, we demonstrate that these observables exhibit distinct patterns depending on whether the sbottom is a scalar (as in supersymmetry) or has spin arising from its UED counterpart. We quantify the statistical significance with which these two hypotheses can be distinguished as a function of integrated luminosity, showing that with sufficient data collected at the LHC, spin correlation measurements can provide a robust and largely model-independent method to determine the true nature of the underlying new physics, complementing cross-section and mass-based analyses. Our results underscore the importance of spin-sensitive observables in the broader program of characterizing new physics discovered at the LHC.

# Abstract

We investigate the prospects for discriminating the spin of a pair-produced colored particle decaying to a bottom quark and a stable, weakly-interacting neutral state, motivated by sbottom pair production followed by the decay $\tilde{b} \to b\,\tilde{\chi}_1^0$ in supersymmetric scenarios. While the observation of such a signature—two $b$-tagged jets accompanied by missing transverse momentum—is a classic hallmark of scalar bottom quark searches, the kinematic distributions alone are generically insufficient to establish that the produced particle is a genuine spin-0 superpartner of the Standard Model bottom quark, as opposed to some other new colored state carrying different spin quantum numbers. We construct a phenomenological comparison between the supersymmetric hypothesis, in which the sbottom is a scalar produced via QCD pair production with subsequent two-body decay to a fermionic neutralino, and an alternative "bosonic" benchmark in which the produced particle carries spin 1 (or, more generally, non-zero spin) while preserving the same production cross section, mass spectrum, and visible decay topology. By analyzing differential distributions sensitive to spin correlations—including the invariant mass and angular separation of the two $b$-jets, the transverse momentum spectrum of the missing energy system, and angular observables constructed in the parton center-of-mass frame—we demonstrate that these two hypotheses yield distinguishable kinematic signatures at parton level, despite sharing identical total cross sections and endpoint structures. We quantify the statistical separation achievable at the LHC for representative mass spectra and integrated luminosities, accounting for detector resolution, combinatorial ambiguities in $b$-jet pairing, and irreducible Standard Model backgrounds such as $t\bar{t}$ and $Z(\to\nu\bar\nu)+b\bar{b}$ production. Our results indicate that with sufficient integrated luminosity, angular and invariant-mass observables in the $b\bar{b}+E_T^{\rm miss}$ final state can provide meaningful discrimination power between the scalar sbottom hypothesis and fermionic or vector-like alternatives, offering a data-driven spin determination that complements direct mass measurements and strengthens the interpretation of any excess in this channel as genuine evidence for supersymmetry.
